knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)

## Section 1: Has provincial reading changed since 2017?

```{r s1-data}
# School average share of students meeting the reading standard, by year.
# 2019 and 2020 stay NA (no tests) so the line breaks there.
trend <- elem |>
  group_by(start_year) |>
  summarise(`Grade 3` = mean(g3_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Grade 6` = mean(g6_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-start_year, names_to = "grade", values_to = "pct") |>
  complete(start_year = 2017:2024, grade)

trend |> filter(!is.na(pct)) |> pivot_wider(names_from = grade, values_from = pct)
```

```{r fig1, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.8}
ggplot(trend, aes(x = start_year, y = pct, colour = grade)) +
  # grey band for the two years without tests
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2018.55, xmax = 2020.45, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey93") +
  annotate("text", x = 2019.5, y = 64, label = "No provincial\ntests\n(COVID-19)",
           size = 3.2, colour = "grey40", lineheight = 0.9) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  # label each line at its right end instead of using a legend
  geom_text(data = filter(trend, start_year == 2024),
            aes(label = paste0(grade, ": ", round(pct), "%")),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.15, size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Grade 3" = "#333333", "Grade 6" = "#8C8C8C"),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2017:2024, labels = year_label(2017:2024),
                     limits = c(2016.8, 2025.6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(60, 92), labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Figure 1. The provincial average barely moves",
       subtitle = "Average share of students meeting the provincial reading standard",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = source_note) +
  theme_story
```

Ontario's reading results have barely changed. In 2017-18, about 74% of Grade 3 students in the average school met the provincial reading standard, and in 2024-25 the figure was still about 74%, 0.1 percentage points lower. Grade 3 dipped after testing resumed in 2021-22 and reached about 71% in 2023-24, roughly 3 points below where it started, before recovering. Grade 6 results are higher and rose from 81% to 85% (Figure 1).

A parent looking at this chart might conclude that nothing has changed. An average can stay flat, though, while some schools improve and others fall behind. To check whether every school stayed the same, we split schools by how many of their students come from low-income households.

## Section 2: How big is the gap between the richest and poorest schools, and is it closing?

```{r s2-data}
# Average reading in the most affluent vs highest-poverty fifth of schools, by year
gap_df <- elem |>
  filter(income_group %in% c("Most affluent fifth", "Highest-poverty fifth")) |>
  group_by(start_year, income_group) |>
  summarise(`Grade 3` = mean(g3_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Grade 6` = mean(g6_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Grade 3`, `Grade 6`), names_to = "grade", values_to = "pct")

# One row per year and grade, with the gap in percentage points
gap_wide <- gap_df |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = income_group, values_from = pct) |>
  mutate(gap = `Most affluent fifth` - `Highest-poverty fifth`)

gap_wide |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !start_year, ~ round(.x, 1)))
```

```{r fig2, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.4}
# Order years so the latest is at the top
gap_plot <- gap_df |>
  mutate(year_lab = factor(year_label(start_year),
                           levels = rev(year_label(sort(unique(start_year))))))
gap_seg <- gap_wide |>
  mutate(year_lab = factor(year_label(start_year), levels = levels(gap_plot$year_lab)))

ggplot() +
  # grey bar = the gap between the two groups
  geom_segment(data = gap_seg,
               aes(y = year_lab, yend = year_lab,
                   x = `Highest-poverty fifth`, xend = `Most affluent fifth`),
               colour = "grey80", linewidth = 2.2) +
  geom_point(data = gap_plot, aes(x = pct, y = year_lab, colour = income_group),
             size = 3.2) +
  # gap size written to the right of each row
  geom_text(data = gap_seg,
            aes(x = `Most affluent fifth` + 1.2, y = year_lab,
                label = paste0(round(gap), " pts")),
            hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "grey25") +
  facet_wrap(~ grade) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = income_cols[c("Most affluent fifth", "Highest-poverty fifth")],
                      name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(58, 97), labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Figure 2. The Grade 3 gap is stuck; the Grade 6 gap is narrowing",
       subtitle = "Share of students meeting the reading standard:\nmost affluent vs highest-poverty fifth of schools",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = source_note) +
  theme_story +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))
```

Once schools are split by income, the flat average hides a steady gap. In 2017-18, 80.5% of Grade 3 students in the most affluent fifth of schools met the reading standard, compared with 64.7% in the highest-poverty fifth, a gap of 15.8 percentage points. In 2024-25 the gap was 15.9 points, and in the years between it stayed between about 14.5 and 16 points (Figure 2). In a class of 30, that is roughly five more children in a high-poverty school who are not reading at the provincial standard.

Grade 6 has changed more. Before the pandemic the gap was about 15 points, the same as in Grade 3. When testing resumed in 2021-22 it had fallen to 11.5 points, and it stayed between about 10 and 13 points through 2024-25, ending at 10.1, about a third smaller than where it started.

The Grade 3 students of 2021-22 were the Grade 6 students of 2024-25. If the gap is fixed in Grade 3 but smaller in Grade 6, do the same children catch up as they get older?

## Section 3: Do students in poorer schools catch up from Grade 3 to Grade 6?

```{r s3-data}
# Follow the same schools: Grade 3 in 2021-22 -> Grade 6 three years later (2024-25).
# Mostly the same class of students. Keep schools with both results.
cohort <- elem |>
  filter(year %in% c("2021-2022", "2024-2025")) |>
  select(school_number, income_group, year, g3_read, g6_read) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = c(g3_read, g6_read)) |>
  transmute(income_group, g3 = `g3_read_2021-2022`, g6 = `g6_read_2024-2025`) |>
  drop_na()

cohort_sum <- cohort |>
  group_by(income_group) |>
  summarise(schools = n(), g3 = mean(g3), g6 = mean(g6), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(gain = g6 - g3)

cohort_sum |> mutate(across(c(g3, g6, gain), ~ round(.x, 1)))
```


```{r fig3, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.6}
# Spread the labels apart so they do not overlap
spread_labels <- function(y, min_gap = 1.9) {
  o <- order(y)
  ys <- y[o]
  for (i in seq_along(ys)[-1]) {
    if (ys[i] - ys[i - 1] < min_gap) ys[i] <- ys[i - 1] + min_gap
  }
  out <- y
  out[o] <- ys
  out
}

cohort_long <- cohort_sum |>
  pivot_longer(c(g3, g6), names_to = "stage", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = c("g3", "g6"),
                        labels = c("Grade 3\n(2021-22)", "Grade 6\n(2024-25)")))
left_lab <- cohort_sum |>
  mutate(y = spread_labels(g3), label = paste0(round(g3), "%"))
right_lab <- cohort_sum |>
  mutate(y = spread_labels(g6),
         label = paste0(round(g6), "%  ", income_group, " (+", round(gain), ")"))

ggplot(cohort_long, aes(x = stage, y = pct, group = income_group, colour = income_group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  geom_text(data = left_lab, aes(x = 1, y = y, label = label), hjust = 1, nudge_x = -0.06,
            size = 3.3, inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = income_cols) +
  geom_text(data = right_lab, aes(x = 2, y = y, label = label), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.06,
            size = 3.3, inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = income_cols) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = income_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.45, 1.75))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Figure 3. Students in high-poverty schools gain the most",
       subtitle = "Same schools, mostly the same students: Grade 3 reading and three years\nlater in Grade 6 (points gained in brackets)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = source_note) +
  theme_story +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

When we follow the same schools for three years, students in poorer schools catch up part of the way. In 2021-22, 61.8% of Grade 3 students in the highest-poverty fifth of schools met the reading standard. In 2024-25, when most of those students wrote the Grade 6 test, 78.7% did, a gain of 16.8 percentage points. The most affluent fifth gained 10.7 points over the same years, from 77.9% to 88.6% (Figure 3). Every income group improved, and the gains grew as school poverty rose, so the gap between the richest and poorest fifth shrank from about 16 points in Grade 3 to about 10 in Grade 6.

The class before them followed the same pattern with smaller gains. From Grade 3 in 2018-19 to Grade 6 in 2021-22, the highest-poverty fifth gained 12.2 points and the most affluent fifth 8.4.

Some of this difference may come from affluent schools having less room to improve, since they were already near 88%. Even so, children in high-poverty schools start Grade 3 well behind. Schools in poorer areas also tend to have more students whose first language is not English. Is language the reason they start behind?


## Methodology and limitations

We used the Ontario Ministry of Education's school information file and kept regular English-language public and Catholic elementary schools: 3,525 schools observed over six school years. Every number in this article is a school's share of students, averaged across schools. A school of 100 students counts the same as a school of 700, and the data say nothing about individual children.

Results are suppressed when fewer than 10 students wrote a test, so small schools often drop out; Grade 3 reading is reported for 18,471 of the 20,836 school-years we kept. No provincial tests were written in 2019-20 or 2020-21, yet the file has values for both years, and 99.9% of the Grade 3 reading values are exact copies of 2018-19, so we dropped those years. The 2023-24 values are stored as proportions (0.73) instead of percentages (73), so we multiplied them by 100.

The low-income measure comes from the census and switches to a newer census in 2022-23, when the median school drops from about 15% to 10%. To compare schools fairly over time, we placed each school in an income fifth using its 2017-18 value and kept it there.

The Grade 3 to Grade 6 comparison needs extra care. Students move between schools, so the same school does not always mean the same children, and affluent schools were already close to 90% in Grade 6, which limits how much they could gain. Across all our comparisons, the test moved online after the pandemic, so results before and after may not be fully comparable.

Student-level EQAO records would show whether the same children really catch up. Weighting results by enrolment would stop small schools from counting as much as large ones, and models that account for school boards could separate neighbourhood income from board-level differences.
